1.title: Governing Data, Training and Testing
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Governing Data, Training and Testing. This is competency B of domain three. A model is only as good, and only as lawful, as the data it learns from and the tests it passes. You will learn how to govern the data, how to plan and run training and testing, and how to keep the records.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Set and follow data governance requirements: lawful rights, quality and fitness. Record lineage and provenance. Plan and run training and testing, including bias, security and interpretability tests. Find and manage issues that appear along the way. And document the work to validate results and show compliance.

1.title: Case Check-In: Whose Data Is This?
1.text: At Helios, Daniel Osei asks Veridex where its hiring tool's training data came from, and the answer is vague. For the customer assistant, Helios will ground answers in its own support documents, which need lineage and quality checks. Mei Tanaka worries about tampering with the document store. Your job is to set the data rules, the test plan and the records.

1.title: Data Governance for AI: The Requirements
1.text: Data governance gives every dataset an owner, rules for use, quality checks, access control, retention and records. A I Act Article ten names eight practices for high-risk training, validation and testing data: design choices, origin and collection, preparation, assumptions, availability and suitability, bias examination, bias mitigation, and gaps. Even outside the A I Act, these are the questions an auditor asks. And governance applies to training, validation and testing data alike. Exam tip: it is the same discipline as for any data, plus bias, representativeness and provenance.

1.title: Lawful Rights to Collect and Use Data
1.text: First, lawful rights. Where did the data come from, and what was the original purpose? On privacy, check the lawful basis, notice, minimization, sensitive-data rules and transfers, from module four. On I P and contract, check licenses, website terms, scraping rules and rights reservations, from module five. For third-party data, get warranties and audit rights. Customer and employee data have contractual limits. And document the assessment before the data are used. Exam tip: if lawful rights are unclear, quality does not matter. Do not use the data.

1.title: Data Quality: The Five Checks
1.text: Five quality checks. Accuracy: values match reality, and labels are right. Completeness: required fields and labels are present. Consistency: the same thing means the same thing across sources. Timeliness: data are current enough for the use, and stale data mislead. Validity: values are in allowed formats and ranges. A I Act Article ten asks for data that are relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors as far as possible, and complete. Exam tip: quality is judged against the purpose. Data fine for reporting can be poor for training.

1.title: Quantity, Representativeness and Fit for Purpose
1.text: How much data is enough? Judge it per group and per condition, not just in total. Representative data reflect the people and settings of real use, including geographic, contextual, behavioral or functional conditions, as Article ten, paragraph four, says. Gaps mean the model may perform worse or unpredictably where data are thin. N I S T also warns that stale or detached data lower trustworthiness. And fit for purpose means the data answer the question the model is meant to answer. Exam tip: a big dataset is not a representative dataset.

1.title: Data Integrity and Protection
1.text: Integrity means the data have not been altered, by accident or attack, since they were approved. Controls include access control, version control, checksums or hashes, secure pipelines and audit trails. Data poisoning is an attack that manipulates training data to change model behavior, and the A I Act names it among the threats to guard against, in Article fifteen. Quarantine new data until checked, and sample and inspect labels. At Helios, the support-document store gets change control and owner approval. Exam tip: whoever can change the data can change the model.

1.title: Lineage: Where Data Came From and What Happened to It
1.text: Lineage is the traceable path of data from source to model: every step, change, owner and version. Why? To reproduce results, find the cause of a problem, remove data on request, and prove compliance. Record at each step who did it, when, what changed, and the version produced. Link each trained model to the exact dataset versions used. Lineage makes deletion and correction requests possible, as module four showed. Exam tip: if you cannot trace which data trained the model, you cannot fix, delete or defend it.

1.title: Provenance: Origin, Rights and Trust
1.text: Provenance is the origin and history of data: who created it, how, when, and on what terms. A provenance record holds the source, the collection method, the date, the license or consent basis, the labeling process and any transformation. For external data, ask the provider for documentation, warranties and audit rights; vague answers are a risk finding. For synthetic data, record the generator and the real data it was based on. At Helios, Veridex must document its provenance before the hiring tool is relied on. Exam tip: provenance is origin and rights. Lineage is what happened afterward.

1.title: Tools and Documents for Lineage and Provenance
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Several tools help. Data catalogs and metadata describe each dataset, its owner and its tags. Data versioning makes each dataset version fixed and identifiable, so models reference versions. Hashes and registries detect unexpected changes. Experiment tracking links data, code, settings and results. Datasheets for datasets are short documents stating a dataset's motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses. And audit trails show who accessed or changed what. Exam tip: a datasheet is to a dataset what a model card is to a model.

1.title: Planning Training and Testing
1.text: Plan before you train. Set the objectives, the data splits, the metrics and thresholds, the test types, and the tools and environments. Define roles and independence: who builds, who tests, and who signs off. N I S T notes that independent review reduces internal bias. Set acceptance criteria: what must be true to move to the next stage. Set thresholds first, as module eight said, so results cannot move the goalposts. And record the plan and any change to it. Exam tip: a test plan written after the results is a report.

1.title: Data Splits, Overfitting and Leakage
1.text: Training data teach the model. Validation data tune settings and choose between models. Test data are held out for a final, unbiased check. Overfitting is when the model memorizes training data and fails on new data. Leakage is when information from the test data, or from the answer, gets into training, so results look better than they are. Split before preprocessing, and use time-based splits when data change over time. Never tune on the test set. Exam tip: a model that scores perfectly on its own training data tells you nothing.

1.title: The Test Types, From Units to Interpretability
1.text: Seven kinds of test. Unit tests check that individual components behave correctly. Integration tests check that components, data pipelines and interfaces work together. Validation tests check that the model meets the requirements for its intended use. Performance tests check accuracy, error rates, speed and stability. Security tests check resistance to attacks and leakage of data. Bias tests check that outcomes are acceptable across groups. And interpretability tests check that reasons can be given to users and overseers. Exam tip: match the test to the risk.

2.title: Bias Testing and Fairness Metrics
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Test by group, including intersections, such as sex and age together. Selection rate and impact ratio compare the rate of selection by group, lower over higher, as in module five. Demographic parity asks for equal selection rates. Equal opportunity asks for equal true-positive rates among people who qualify. Equalized odds asks for equal true-positive and false-positive rates. These cannot all be satisfied at once in most real settings, so choose by context and record why. N I S T Measure two point eleven asks that fairness and bias be evaluated and documented. Exam tip: removing the protected attribute does not make a model fair.

2.title: Mitigating Bias: Before, During and After Training
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Bias can be reduced at three points. Before training: collect more representative data, re-sample or re-weight, fix labels and remove proxies. During training: add fairness constraints or objectives. After training: adjust thresholds, where lawful, add human review, and keep monitoring. Retest after each change and record the trade-offs with accuracy. Some adjustments by group can raise legal questions, so involve legal first. At Helios, the proxy features were removed and the model recalibrated, and the ratio rose to zero point nine one. Exam tip: fixing the data usually beats patching the outputs.

2.title: Security and Interpretability Testing
2.text: Security and interpretability tests need their own attention. Adversarial testing uses inputs built to cause mistakes, and prompts built to break rules for language models. Data poisoning checks look for manipulated or suspicious training records. Privacy leakage tests ask whether the model can reveal or reproduce training data or personal information. Robustness tests check noise, drift and unusual inputs. Interpretability tests ask whether overseers and users can get reasons. The A I Act names poisoning, adversarial examples and confidentiality attacks in Article fifteen. Exam tip: security testing is separate from accuracy testing.

2.title: Common Issues in Training and Testing
2.text: Six common issues. Overfitting: great on training data, poor on new data, so simplify, add data, or regularize. Leakage: suspiciously high scores, so fix the split and retest. Label errors: inconsistent labels, so audit and relabel. Unrepresentative data: poor results for some groups, so collect more or re-sample. Poisoning: odd records or behavior, so quarantine and investigate. And unlawful or unclear rights: stop, quarantine and escalate. Exam tip: read the symptom in the question, and pick the response that fits it.

2.title: Managing Issues: Log, Triage, Fix, Retest
2.text: Manage issues in four moves. Log every issue with its severity and owner. Triage: does it affect people, legality or safety? Those go up first. Find the root cause and fix it by changing data, features, the model or the process. Retest and record that the issue is closed, and escalate what cannot be fixed. Unresolved high-severity issues block the next stage. If unlawfully obtained data are found, quarantine them and ask legal and privacy for a decision. Exam tip: unresolved lawfulness questions stop the line.

2.title: Risks of Pretrained, Generative and Third-Party Models
2.text: Pretrained and third-party models carry their own risks. A foundation model brings its own bias, data rights and memorization risks. Fine-tuning can add new data issues and can weaken safety behaviors. Benchmark contamination means test items may have been in the model's training data, so scores look inflated. Retrieval data, as at Helios, need quality, rights and freshness controls. And ask vendors for test reports, data documentation and known limitations, then verify key claims with your own tests. Exam tip: buying a model does not remove your duty to test it.

2.title: Documenting Training and Testing
2.text: Document training and testing to validate results, show compliance, manage risk, and let others reproduce the work. For data: sources, versions, splits, lineage and provenance. For training: methods, settings, experiments and tools. For testing: the test plan, metrics and thresholds, results by group, issues found and fixed, and sign-offs. And the decisions: why this model, this threshold and this trade-off. N I S T Measure two point one asks that test sets, metrics and tool details be documented. Exam tip: a result without its data version cannot be defended.

2.title: Model Cards and Test Reports
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. A model card is a short document that accompanies a model: its intended use, performance across groups, the conditions of evaluation, and its limitations. It links to the datasheet for the training data. It helps deployers know what the model can and cannot do. The A I Act's Annex four asks for similar detail: data requirements, validation and testing with metrics, and discriminatory impacts. At Helios, the team asks Veridex for a model card and checks it against its own results. Exam tip: state where the model works and where it does not.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Data rules: lawful rights first, then quality, representativeness and integrity, with protection against tampering. Lineage and provenance: trace data from source to model, and record origin, rights and changes. Training and testing: plan first, split data properly, run the tests from unit to interpretability, test bias by group, and mitigate before, during and after training. Issues: log, triage, fix, retest, and stop on unresolved high severity or unclear rights. Records: data, methods, metrics, results by group, decisions, datasheets and model cards.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Daniel Osei wants to use Helios's past support tickets to ground the customer assistant. Which check must come first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Lawful rights come first: if Helios may not use the tickets for this purpose, quality and tuning do not matter. The tickets contain personal data and may carry confidentiality terms.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which two checks assess the quality and fitness for purpose of data for a hiring screening model? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Fitness depends on how representative the data are for the real population and setting, and on error and completeness rates in values and labels. Compute, storage price and transfer speed are operational matters.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A vendor cannot say where the data used to train its tool came from. What is the best governance response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Provenance determines whether the data may be used and what risks they carry, so missing documentation is a finding. Ask for documentation, warranties and audit rights, and avoid high-risk reliance until it is resolved.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Which practice best prevents data leakage when evaluating a model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Leakage happens when information from the test data reaches training or tuning. Splitting first and leaving the test set untouched until the final check keeps the result unbiased. The other practices mix the sets and inflate results.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Helios will test the hiring tool for bias. Which two actions fit? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Bias testing compares outcomes and errors across groups, including intersections. Overall accuracy can hide group gaps, removing an attribute leaves proxies, and testing on training data says nothing about new applicants.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. During training, a team learns that part of its dataset was scraped in breach of the source's terms. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Data with unclear or breached rights are a stop-the-line issue. Quarantine them, escalate, and decide with legal and privacy on removal and retraining. Continuing, deleting records or hiding the source makes it worse.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which content best belongs in a model card? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A model card states what the model is for, how it was evaluated, how it performs across groups, and where it falls short. Marketing material, secrets and personal data do not belong in it.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: C. Question two: B and D. Question three: D. Question four: A. Question five: C and E. Question six: B. Question seven: D. That completes Module nine. Next, Module ten covers governing release, monitoring and maintenance.
